claim: Gerbils display primate-like magnitude estimation characteristics in time reproduction.
source: We show that gerbils display primate-like magnitude estimation characteristics in time reproduction.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing regression effects and scalar variability in gerbil time reproduction performance

claim: Gerbils show systematic overestimation of small stimuli and underestimation of large stimuli in time reproduction (regression effect).
source: Most prominently their behavioral responses show a systematic overestimation of small stimuli and an underestimation of large stimuli, often referred to as regression effect.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1D showing reproductions deviate from unity line

claim: The majority of medial prefrontal cortex neurons respond either during the measurement or the reproduction of a time interval.
source: We investigated the underlying neural mechanisms by recording from medial prefrontal cortex and show that the majority of neurons respond either during the measurement or the reproduction of a time interval.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing 16% active only during measurement, 23% only during reproduction, and 17% in both phases

claim: Cells that are active during both measurement and reproduction phases display distinct response patterns.
source: Cells that are active during both phases display distinct response patterns.
evidence: Demonstrated by single-cell recordings showing different firing patterns between task phases

claim: Only populations with mixed responses can encode the bias of the regression effect.
source: We categorize the neural responses into multiple types and demonstrate that only populations with mixed responses can encode the bias of the regression effect.
evidence: Shown through decoding analysis demonstrating that mixing linear increasing and slope-changing neurons produces regression effects

claim: The regression effect may be the result of an error minimization strategy.
source: Recently, this bias regained attention as it may be the result of an error minimization strategy (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Petzschner and Glasauer, 2011; Cicchini et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work

claim: The coefficient of variation correlated with the strength of regression in gerbil behavior.
source: The CV correlated with the strength of regression, indicating a connection between the regression effect and error minimization (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1F

claim: The average width of the feedback range in a session correlated negatively with the slope.
source: Since we adapted the feedback range after every stimulus (Figure 1B), its width indicated estimation precision, with a narrower feedback range corresponding to higher precision. The average width of the feedback range in a session correlated negatively with the slope, which is another sign of a connection between the regression effect and error minimization (Figure 1F).
evidence: Shown by correlation analysis in Figure 1F

claim: A total of 1766 mPFC units were recorded over 101 experimental sessions from three gerbils.
source: We recorded a total of 1766 mPFC units over 101 experimental sessions from three gerbils.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data collection

claim: No single cell responded in the very same way in both measurement and reproduction task phases.
source: We did not find a single cell that responded in the very same way in both task phases and essentially repeated its activity pattern from the measurement phase during reproduction – an observation that will be analyzed systematically below.
evidence: Based on systematic analysis of single-cell responses across task phases

claim: Virtual speed significantly modulated 22% of neurons and running speed significantly modulated 27% of neurons.
source: Although also weak speed modulation could be significant, it was significant in only 22% of the neurons for virtual speed and in 27% for the running speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Shown by speed response function analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Population activity correlated for different stimuli during reproduction but not during measurement.
source: Neural activity was similar for different stimulus durations during reproduction. On the one hand, population activity correlated for different stimuli (Figure 3F2); on the other hand, single-neuron activity correlated across different stimuli in about 20% of the neurons (Figure 3G2). During measurement, correlations across stimuli were absent (Figure 3F1 and G1).
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F and 3G

claim: Correlating population vectors in corresponding time bins for measurement and reproduction yielded only low values.
source: Also, correlating population vectors in corresponding time bins for measurement and reproduction yielded only low values (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by population vector correlation analysis in Figure 3D

claim: For single cells, the correlation between measurement and reproduction task phases was significant in about 20% of the cells.
source: For single cells, however, the correlation between task phases was larger and significant in about 20% of the cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by single-cell correlation analysis in Figure 3E

claim: Centers of mass of spike density functions were widely distributed and tiled the time intervals during reproduction.
source: The COMs were, in particular during reproduction, widely distributed and tiled the time intervals.
evidence: Shown by center of mass analysis in Figure 4A

claim: Centers of mass for recorded spike density functions significantly differed from noise controls in all cases (p<0.001).
source: The corresponding COMs clustered around the center of the intervals and significantly differed from those for the recorded SDFs (p<0.001 in all cases, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 4A).
evidence: Statistical testing using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shown in Figure 4A

claim: During reproduction, neurons with center of mass at the begin or end of an interval showed stronger correlation of activity across different stimuli.
source: Interestingly, during reproduction, for neurons with a COM at the begin or end of an interval, activity correlated more strongly across different stimuli (Figure 4B, Figure 3G2).
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis as a function of center of mass in Figure 4B

claim: Scaling indices during reproduction were close to theoretical values and even larger or smaller than prediction in a manner consistent with the regression effect.
source: Indeed, scaling indices were close to the theoretical values during both measurement and reproduction (Figure 4C and D). During reproduction, scaling indices were even larger or smaller than the prediction in a manner consistent with the regression effect, that is, smaller durations had larger scaling factors and vice versa.
evidence: Shown by scaling index analysis in Figure 4C and D

claim: Bootstrapped Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests showed p-values below 0.05 for almost all cases during reproduction.
source: The p-values obtained lay below 0.05 for almost all cases during reproduction.
evidence: Statistical testing results from bootstrapped analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: During measurement, only about 30% of bootstrapped Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests were significant.
source: During measurement, only about 30% of the bootstrapped Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests were significant (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical testing results shown in Figure 4E

claim: The principal components for measurement and reproduction shared common features.
source: Interestingly, the PCs for measurement and reproduction shared common features (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by demixed PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: The time course-related principal components were ramp-like (PC 1) or had a comparable non-monotonous shape (PC 2 and 3).
source: The time course-related PCs were ramp-like (PC 1) or had a comparable non-monotonous shape (PC 2 and 3).
evidence: Shown by demixed PCA results in Figure 5A and B

claim: The strongest stimulus-dependent principal component was constant over time and had amplitudes ordered by stimulus.
source: The strongest stimulus-dependent PC was constant over time and had amplitudes that were ordered by stimulus (see bottom-right panels in Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Shown in demixed PCA analysis in Figure 5A and B

claim: The contribution of the principal components to single-cell responses (PCA scores) correlated for PC 1 and stimulus PC 1 in both measurement and reproduction.
source: Moreover, the contribution of the PCs to the single-cell responses (PCA scores) correlated for PC 1 and stimulus PC 1, indicating a link between ramp-like and stimulus-dependent activity in both measurement and reproduction (Figure 5C, see also Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by PCA score correlation analysis in Figure 5C

claim: In the measurement phase, PCs 2 and 3 contributed very little to explaining population activity; instead, PCs were most strongly driven by stimulus duration.
source: In the measurement phase, PCs 2 and 3 in general contributed very little to explaining population activity; instead, PCs were most strongly driven by stimulus duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by explained variance analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: During reproduction but not during measurement, stimulus PC 1 correlated with PCs 2 and 3.
source: During reproduction but not during measurement, stimulus PC 1 also correlated with PCs 2 and 3, arguing for a richer representation of the to-be-reproduced compared to the to-be-measured time interval.
evidence: Shown by PC correlation analysis in Figure 5C

claim: In the measurement phase, neural activity developed at similar speed along trajectories with a length that depended on stimulus duration.
source: Indeed, in the measurement phase, neural activity developed at similar speed along trajectories with a length that depended on stimulus duration.
evidence: Shown by conventional PCA trajectory analysis in Figure 5D

claim: During reproduction, trajectories had similar length but activity along those trajectories accelerated over an interval resulting in higher average speed for stimuli of shorter duration.
source: During reproduction, trajectories had similar length. However, activity along those trajectories accelerated over an interval resulting at higher average speed for stimuli of shorter duration.
evidence: Shown by conventional PCA trajectory analysis in Figure 5E

claim: During measurement, PC 1 of the original data was larger than expected from surrogate data.
source: During measurement, PC 1 of the original data was larger than expected, suggesting that collective activity added to representing ongoing time; similarly, PC 3 was larger than expected during reproduction (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Shown by comparison to tensor maximum entropy surrogate data in Figure 5—figure supplement 6

claim: Stimulus PC 1 was stronger than expected in reproduction, indicating that the population as a whole contributed to the representation of the stimulus interval.
source: Stimulus PC 1 was stronger than expected in reproduction, indicating that here the population as a whole contributed to the representation of the stimulus interval.
evidence: Shown by comparison to tensor maximum entropy surrogate data in Figure 5—figure supplement 6

claim: About a quarter of cells showed ramping activity during measurement.
source: During measurement, about a quarter of the cells showed such ramping activity.
evidence: Determined from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: About 10% of neurons showed ramping activity (PC 1 only) during reproduction.
source: During reproduction, about 10% of the neurons showed ramping activity (PC 1 only), for example, ramp-to-threshold cells where the rate of ramping decreased with stimulus duration (examples in Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Determined from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: About 10% of neurons during reproduction were explained by mixing PCs 1 and 2, and 6% by a mixture of PCs 1–3.
source: Another ∼10% of neurons were explained by mixing PCs 1 and 2, and 6% by a mixture of PCs 1–3.
evidence: Determined from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: About 5% of neurons during reproduction combined ramps with stimulus duration-dependent firing.
source: However, counting all combinations of stimulus PC 1 with PCs 1–3 showed that about 5% of the neurons combined ramps with stimulus duration-dependent firing.
evidence: Determined from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: In total, 35% of cells during reproduction contained a ramping component.
source: In total, 35% of the cells contained a ramping component.
evidence: Calculated from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Half of the ramping neurons were significantly modulated by virtual speed and 60% by running speed.
source: Half of the ramping neurons were significantly modulated by virtual speed and 60% by running speed.
evidence: Determined from speed response function analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Speed modulation indices were in general low for ramping cells.
source: Nevertheless, speed modulation indices were in general low for those ramping cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Shown by modulation index analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: About 17% of cells fired action potentials in both measurement and reproduction phases, 16% were only active during measurement and 23% only during reproduction; 44% of cells did not contribute substantially in either phase.
source: About 17% of the cells fired action potentials in both phases, 16% were only active during measurement and 23% only during reproduction; 44% of the cells did not contribute substantially in either phase (pie chart in Figure 6D).
evidence: Determined from categorization analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: During the reproduction phase, time readouts were accurate in the first seconds but by the end of the phase a regression effect was visible with over- and underestimation at short and long stimuli.
source: During the reproduction phase, time readouts were accurate in the first seconds; however, by the end of the phase, a regression effect was visible with over- and underestimation at short and long stimuli, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: Shown by linear regression decoding analysis in Figure 7A

claim: Neurons that ramp to stimulus-dependent levels but with the same slope show precise time representation but no regression effect.
source: Decoding time from neurons that ramp with same slope to stimulus duration-dependent levels (linear increasing neurons) shows precise time representation but no regression effect (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical simulation and decoding from categorized neurons in Figure 7B

claim: Ramp-to-threshold cells that change slope but reach same activity levels by the end of an interval can only encode the mean of the stimulus distribution and result in maximal regression.
source: Whereas ramp-to-threshold cells that change slope but reach same activity levels by the end of an interval can only encode the mean of the stimulus distribution and result in maximal regression (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical simulation and decoding from categorized neurons in Figure 7C

claim: The more slope-changing cells present in the population, the stronger the regression effect.
source: The more slope-changing cells were present in the population, the stronger was the regression effect (top-right panel in Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by decoding from mixed populations with varying fractions in Figure 7F

claim: A population of neurons that are phasically active at different absolute times tiling the whole interval would provide an accurate time representation.
source: In contrast, a population of neurons that are phasically active at different absolute times tiling the whole interval would provide an accurate time representation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical simulation in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Neurons that are active relative to the stimulus interval can only encode a single time point.
source: Constructing again theoretical stereotypes, we saw that neurons that are active relative to the stimulus interval can only encode a single time point.
evidence: Demonstrated by theoretical simulation in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: During measurement, time decoding was imprecise with overestimation at the begin and underestimation at the end of the interval.
source: Here, decoding was imprecise with overestimation at the begin and underestimation at the end of the interval (Figure 7—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Shown by decoding analysis during measurement in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: When decoding time from cells in the PC 1-only category during measurement, a regression effect was seen.
source: Interestingly, when we decoded time from the cells in the PC 1-only category, a regression effect was also seen during measurement (rightmost panel in Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting an impact of previous stimuli (prior knowledge) on the activity of these neurons already during stimulus measurement and not just during reproduction.
evidence: Shown by decoding analysis from PC 1-only cells in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: The mPFC responses recorded during the reproduction phase are reminiscent of neural correlates of self-initiated behavior found in rat secondary motor cortex.
source: The mPFC responses we recorded during the reproduction phase are reminiscent of the neural correlates of self-initiated behavior found in rat secondary motor cortex by Murakami et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017.
evidence: Comparison to previously published findings

claim: Ramp-to-threshold responses have been found in monkey motor cortices during various timing behaviors.
source: Ramp-to-threshold responses have also been found in monkey motor cortices during various timing behaviors (Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006; Mita et al., 2009; Merchant et al., 2011) and as a population pattern in lateral intraparietal cortex (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015) during time (re-)production, demonstrating their ubiquitous presence in self-initiated behaviors.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Linear increasing neurons may serve as integrators of time information provided by sequentially activated, phasically responding cells.
source: In addition, we observed linear increasing neurons (neurons that ramp to stimulus duration-dependent levels at the same slope, e.g., Figure 2B) that may serve as integrators of time information provided by sequentially activated, phasically responding cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on observed neural responses and inference about their function

claim: Responses with a linear ramping component have been shown to be important for precise time decoding and to underlie low-dimensional population dynamics.
source: Responses with a linear ramping component (comprising both linear increasing and ramp-to-threshold) have been shown to be important for precise time decoding and to underlie low-dimensional population dynamics (Cueva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Temporal scaling appears to be a general feature of timed computations in the brain as it has been described in various brain regions.
source: Temporal scaling appears to be a general feature of timed computations in the brain as it has been described in various brain regions (Xu et al., 2014; Mello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Temporal scaling has been demonstrated to be important for time coding in neural network models.
source: It has also been demonstrated to be important for time coding in neural network models (Bi and Zhou, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to modeling study

claim: In the experiments, neuronal activity scaled and changed speed in relation to the stimulus duration in the reproduction phase only.
source: In our experiments, neuronal activity scaled and changed speed in relation to the stimulus duration in the reproduction phase only.
evidence: Based on scaling analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Temporal scaling and speed dependence of neural dynamics corresponded to the regression effect observed in the behavioral data.
source: Temporal scaling and speed dependence of neural dynamics corresponded to the regression effect we observed in the behavioral data.
evidence: Based on comparison of neural scaling patterns and behavioral regression effects

claim: Bayesian models have demonstrated that the regression effect may be a strategy to minimize behavioral errors.
source: Bayesian models (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Petzschner et al., 2015) as well as other approaches (Bausenhart et al., 2014; Thurley, 2016) have demonstrated that the regression effect may be a strategy to minimize behavioral errors.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous modeling studies

claim: Curved state-space trajectories during measurement can be interpreted as a compressed nonlinear representation of time, which when read-out appropriately during reproduction can explain regression effects seen in behavior.
source: These curved trajectories can be interpreted as a compressed nonlinear representation of time, which when read-out appropriately during reproduction can explain regression effects seen in behavior.
evidence: Based on interpretation of findings from Sohn et al., 2019

claim: The demixed PCs showed curved trajectories during measurement.
source: Our demixed PCs also showed curved trajectories during measurement (Figure 5A)
evidence: Shown by demixed PCA analysis in Figure 5A

claim: Trajectories from conventional PCA did not comprise curvatures during measurement.
source: however, trajectories from conventional PCA did not comprise such curvatures (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Shown by conventional PCA analysis in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A

claim: Curved state-space trajectories were observed in the reproduction phase.
source: The fact that we observed curved state-space trajectories in the reproduction phase suggests this possibility.
evidence: Based on PCA trajectory analysis during reproduction

claim: Without noise, duration encoding is dominated by neurons that ramp with a constant slope and no regression effect emerges.
source: Without noise, duration encoding is dominated by neurons that ramp with a constant slope and no regression effect emerges.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about mixed population responses

claim: If activity is noisy, neurons with stimulus-dependent slope contribute and the regression effect appears.
source: If activity is noisy, neurons with stimulus-dependent slope contribute and the regression effect appears.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about mixed population responses

claim: The amount of noise (uncertainty about the current stimulus) determines the impact of either response type and thus the balance between current stimulus estimate and prior knowledge.
source: Thus, the amount of noise (uncertainty about the current stimulus) determines the impact of either response type and thus the balance between current stimulus estimate and prior knowledge.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about mixed population responses

claim: State-space trajectories for different stimulus durations were well separated during measurement.
source: State-space trajectories for different stimulus durations were well separated during measurement (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by demixed PCA analysis in Figure 5A

claim: Duration-dependent trajectories during measurement are likely due to prior expectations about the stimulus duration.
source: Since stimulus duration is unknown at the beginning of the measurement phase, such duration-dependent trajectories are likely due to prior expectations about the stimulus duration.
evidence: Based on inference from observed trajectory separation

claim: Sequential effects are known in magnitude estimation.
source: Such sequential effects are known in magnitude estimation (Bausenhart et al., 2014; Petzschner et al., 2015; Thurley, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Influences of prior expectations on neural activity during time interval estimation have been reported recently.
source: Influences of prior expectations on neural activity during time interval estimation have been reported recently (Meirhaeghe et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work

claim: During reproduction, trajectories were ordered by stimulus, which is considered an indication that cortical dynamics are adjusted for (re-)producing different time intervals.
source: During reproduction, trajectories were also ordered by stimulus (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 5B), which is considered an indication that cortical dynamics are adjusted for (re-)producing different time intervals (Remington et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on PCA trajectory analysis and citation to previous work

claim: Variables underlying cognitive functions may be encoded by mixed responses within a local neural population.
source: This reveals that variables underlying cognitive functions may be encoded by mixed responses within a local neural population.
evidence: Based on findings about mixed response types encoding regression effect

claim: Stimulus intervals were randomly sampled between 3 and 7.5 s.
source: Intervals were randomly sampled between 3 and 7.5 s.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: The task was implemented in virtual reality which gave the use of a treadmill, prevented landmark-based strategies for task-solving and decoupled time from distance.
source: The task was implemented in a rodent virtual reality system (Thurley and Ayaz, 2017), which (1) gave us the use of a treadmill, (2) prevented landmark-based strategies for task-solving and (3) decoupled time from distance, such that the task could not be solved by path integration.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design rationale

claim: Gerbils were used because they could be successfully trained in complex virtual reality tasks before.
source: We used gerbils because we could successfully train these animals in complex virtual reality tasks before (Thurley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Timing experiments with gerbils in virtual reality or alike have been performed by the authors and others.
source: We and others also performed timing experiments with gerbils in virtual reality (Kautzky and Thurley, 2016) or alike (Shankar and Ellard, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The mPFC is a brain area that has been implicated in interval timing in rodents and other species.
source: Then, we present associated neural activity in gerbil medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) – a brain area that has been implicated in interval timing in rodents and other species (Genovesio et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014; Emmons et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The activity observed was composed of mixtures of responses including phasic activation and ramp-like firing patterns, response types well known from the interval timing literature.
source: The activity we observed was composed of mixtures of responses including phasic activation and ramp-like firing patterns, response types well known from the interval timing literature (e.g., Mita et al., 2009; Merchant et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2013; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Paton and Buonomano, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Human studies identified frontal, parietal, and striatal brain regions that are active during magnitude estimation.
source: Human studies identified frontal, parietal, and striatal brain regions that are active during magnitude estimation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from human neuroimaging

claim: Recent studies with nonhuman primates used time interval reproduction experiments to investigate the connection between neural population dynamics in frontal and parietal cortices and magnitude estimation behavior.
source: Recent studies with nonhuman primates used time interval reproduction experiments to investigate the connection between neural population dynamics in frontal and parietal cortices and magnitude estimation behavior (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015; Sohn et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent primate studies

claim: Previous primate studies focused on the estimation of time intervals lasting hundreds of milliseconds.
source: These studies focused on the estimation of time intervals lasting hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: Based on description of previous primate studies

claim: It is unclear how findings from primate studies on short intervals translate to durations of several seconds.
source: What remains unclear is how their findings translate to durations of several seconds, that is, to time scales that are relevant for more complex and ecologically important behaviors like spatial navigation and action planning.
evidence: Identification of gap in knowledge

claim: It is unresolved to what extent the results from primate studies generalize to nonprimate species.
source: Furthermore, it is unresolved to what extent the results generalize to nonprimate species.
evidence: Identification of gap in knowledge

claim: It is an ongoing debate whether a dedicated or distributed magnitude system exists in the brain.
source: It is an ongoing debate whether a dedicated or distributed magnitude system exists in the brain (for review, see Cohen Kadosh et al., 2008; Bueti and Walsh, 2009; Opstal and Verguts, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: Neural correlates of interval timing in the range of seconds have been found in several brain areas including prefrontal cortex, pre-/supplementary motor cortex, hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and striatum.
source: Neural correlates of interval timing in the range of seconds have been found in several brain areas (Merchant et al., 2013; Paton and Buonomano, 2018; Issa et al., 2020), including prefrontal cortex (Genovesio et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014; Emmons et al., 2017; Tiganj et al., 2017), pre-/supplementary motor cortex (Mita et al., 2009; Merchant et al., 2011), hippocampus (MacDonald et al., 2011), entorhinal cortex (Heys and Dombeck, 2018), and striatum (Gouvêa et al., 2015; Mello et al., 2015; Bakhurin et al., 2017; Emmons et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The experiments tested time intervals on a continuous range.
source: What distinguishes our experiments from previous studies is twofold: (1) we tested time intervals on a continuous range
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: The experiments combined timing of an external event (measurement phase) and timing own behavior (reproduction phase), linking sensory and motor timing.
source: and (2) we combined timing of an external event (measurement phase) and timing own behavior (reproduction phase), linking sensory and motor timing (Paton and Buonomano, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: The study is conceptually different from the fixed interval or discrimination tasks that have been used in most previous timing studies.
source: Our study is therefore conceptually different from the fixed interval or discrimination tasks that have been used in most of the above timing studies.
evidence: Comparison to previous experimental approaches

claim: The neural activity in primate parietal and frontal cortices observed in previous studies is surprisingly similar to what was found in rodent mPFC.
source: The neural activity in primate parietal and frontal cortices observed in these studies is surprisingly similar to what we found in rodent mPFC.
evidence: Comparison of current findings to previous primate studies

claim: Neural dynamics typically act on much shorter time scales than several seconds.
source: This is especially interesting since we tested timing of several seconds and neural dynamics typically act on much shorter time scales.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about neural dynamics

claim: Murakami et al. reported the absence of ramp-to-threshold responses in mPFC during waiting tasks.
source: However, in contrast to our findings, they reported the absence of such responses in mPFC (Murakami et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The discrepancy between the current findings and Murakami et al. may be due to different tasks involved.
source: This discrepancy may be due to the different tasks involved: waiting for a signal to appear after a random interval in their experiments vs. responding after a previously measured interval in our case.
evidence: Inference about source of discrepancy with previous study

claim: Mixed response types are important in cognitive tasks.
source: Mixed response types are in general important in cognitive tasks (Rigotti et al., 2013) but have also been reported during spontaneous behavior (Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Coding of variables related to cognitive functions like choice and task engagement is often distributed across brain regions.
source: Coding of variables related to cognitive functions like choice and task engagement is often distributed across brain regions (Steinmetz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The experiments were conducted with three female adult Mongolian gerbils from a wild-type colony.
source: The experiments in this study were conducted with three female adult Mongolian gerbils (M. unguiculatus) from a wild-type colony at the local animal house (referred to by IDs 10526, 11769, and 11770 throughout the article).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental subjects

claim: Training started at an age of at least 4 months.
source: Training started at an age of at least 4 months.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: The gerbils were housed individually on a 12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: The gerbils were housed individually on a 12 hr light/dark cycle, and all behavioral training and recording sessions were performed in the light phase of the cycle.
evidence: Direct statement of housing conditions

claim: The animals received a diet maintaining them at about 85–95% of their free feeding weight.
source: The animals received a diet maintaining them at about 85–95% of their free feeding weight.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure

claim: All experiments were approved according to national and European guidelines on animal welfare.
source: All experiments were approved according to national and European guidelines on animal welfare (Reg. von Oberbayern, District Government of Upper Bavaria; reference numbers: AZ 55.2-1-54-2532-10-11 and AZ 55.2-1-54-2532-70-2016).
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval
